paper.code_data_availability: Data availability (page 5), verbatim: ‘‘For R/Stata do files, see http://www.ludovisschers.eu and https://edatos.consorciomadrono.es The miscoding correction matrix will be there as well. …

registers.name_in_paper: the wage payment records in Danish administrative data, the ‘‘Beskæftigelse for lønmodtagere’’ (BFL) database
registers.role: sample frame, treatment and outcome measurement for the Danish arm: employment spells, employer switches and occupation
variables_mentioned: job spell start and end dates (wage payment records)

registers.name_in_paper: the monthly Current Population Survey (CPS) provided by IPUMS (Flood et al., 2023)
registers.role: comparison country: EE movers, origin and destination occupation for the United States

registers.name_in_paper: the crosswalk between ISCO08 and the US 2010 standard occupation classification (SOC), provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics
registers.role: linkage: harmonization of Danish DISCO08/ISCO08 occupations to the US OCC1990 classification

registers.name_in_paper: the estimate of the miscoding probabilities from our companion paper (Carrillo-Tudela et al., 2025)
registers.role: correction of the US three-digit occupational flow matrix for occupational miscoding

linkages: Danish occupations (DISCO08, very similar to ISCO08) mapped via the BLS ISCO08–SOC2010 crosswalk into IPUMS' OCC1990 1990 Census classification

A reverse SOC-to-ISCO crosswalk step merges each ‘‘orphaned’’ SOC code into a non-orphaned SOC code, yielding 209 occupations present in both countries (‘‘three digit’’), which are then aggregated to two- and one-digit levels (13 major occupations)

Danish employment spells constructed from wage payment records and chained across employers to identify EE transitions; occupation measured as the last recorded occupation of the previous spell and the first of the subsequent spell
US corrected flows obtained by inverting the estimated miscoding matrix at the three-digit level, then aggregated to two- and one-digit classifications

sample.universe: Employer-to-employer (‘EE’) movers in Denmark and in the United States, 2011–2019, excluding military occupations
sample.unit_of_observation: Occupation (for the Panel A averages, the Panel B regressions and the figures); EE transition (for constructing the underlying mobility rates)
selection_rules: Denmark: wage payment records (BFL) 2011–2019 — the period is chosen because of a change in occupational classification in 2010
Denmark: workers in military occupations excluded
Denmark: an employer switch without intervening nonemployment (‘‘EE transition’’) is recorded when a new job spell starts within two months of the end of the previous job spell
Denmark: missing occupation data filled with the mode occupation of a given worker–firm spell
United States: EE movers are those employed in two consecutive months who report having changed employer
United States: both the origin and destination job must be salaried; military occupations excluded
Both countries: occupations harmonized to the 209-occupation classification (three digit), aggregated to two- and one-digit levels
Occupation-level regressions (Table 1 Panel B) and Fig. 2: only occupations with at least 100 (unweighted) observations in each country
Table 1 Panel A: all occupations used, including the few with negative weights or negative gross mobility after the miscoding correction

construction_notes: Gross mobility m(i) = f_out(i)/ee(i) and net mobility n_r(i) = (1/2)[f_in(i) − f_out(i)]/[f_in(i) + f_out(i)], Eq. (1), where ee(i) is total EE flows originating from occupation i and f_in(i), f_out(i) are total flows in and out of occupation i
Occupational stays (self-flows) are included in both f_in(i) and f_out(i) unless a statistic is explicitly labelled 'excl self'
Table 1 Panel A reports the average of the ABSOLUTE net mobility rate
The resulting monthly Danish EE transition rate is 1.1% (footnote 3 notes Bertheau and Vejlin (2022) find 1.2% for a similar period and sample)

US flows corrected for occupational miscoding using the matrix from Carrillo-Tudela et al. (2025): corrected flow matrix recovered by inverting the estimated miscoding matrix at the three-digit level, then aggregated upwards
The ISCO–SOC mapping is many-to-many; selecting a unique Census occupation per ISCO code results in 78 fewer Census occupations, so a reverse crosswalk step is used to merge orphaned SOC codes
Panel A statistics are population-weighted over all occupations; Panel B regressions weight each occupation by sqrt( N^DK(i)/Σ N^DK(i) · N^US(i)/Σ N^US(i) )
Fig. 2 panels (c) and (f) collect the more than 200 three-digit occupations into 20 bins ranked by Danish mobility rates
Danish occupational mobility is measured only across employers; occupational mobility within employer is explicitly ignored
Excluding the mode-imputed Danish occupations moves the overall occupation-switching propensity of EE movers from 0.2942 to 0.2934 (footnote 5)

claims.statement: At the one-digit aggregation level, the average gross occupational mobility rate of Danish EE movers (0.22) is lower than the miscoding-corrected US rate (0.28).

key_assumptions.assumption: The harmonized crosswalk makes Danish (DISCO08/ISCO08) and US (OCC1990) occupation categories measure the same occupations, so that an occupation change means the same thing in both countries
key_assumptions.supported_by: Construction of a 209-occupation classification in which every worker in both countries is assigned an occupation and every occupation is present in both countries, using the BLS ISCO08–SOC crosswalk plus a reverse SOC-to-ISCO step; the paper shows that skipping the reverse step makes Danish mobility falsely appear comparatively lower

key_assumptions.assumption: Danish employer-reported occupations are measured with very little error
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional argument only: legal requirements on non-small firms to report annual earnings by occupation, on large firms to report wages by gender and six-digit occupation, and access to the migration-focused ‘Positive List’; no validation exercise is performed

key_assumptions.assumption: The miscoding-probability matrix estimated in the companion paper correctly characterizes US occupational miscoding, so that inverting it recovers the true US occupational flow matrix

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the note to Table 1

threats_discussed: Occupational miscoding in the US CPS (independent interviewing) creates spurious flows that bias raw mobility measures upwards
The many-to-many ISCO–SOC crosswalk leaves US occupations ‘‘orphaned’’ with no Danish counterpart, which makes Danish mobility falsely appear comparatively lower
Differences in the occupational composition of EE movers between the two countries could drive the aggregate mobility gap
Missing occupation data in the Danish records (filled with the mode occupation of the worker–firm spell)
Different occupational classifications (DISCO08/ISCO08 vs OCC1990) in the two countries
robustness_checks: US statistics reported both corrected and uncorrected for occupational miscoding

All statistics reported at one-, two- and three-digit aggregation levels

Occupation-level relationship estimated in levels and in logs
Occupations with fewer than 100 unweighted observations in either country excluded from the occupation-level regressions and from Fig. 2
unresolved_confounders: The lower propensity of Danish EE movers to switch careers might be compensated or offset by a higher occupation-switching propensity of unemployed workers, or of workers who change occupations while staying with the same employer — left for future research (footnote 8)
